title: the breath again — every claim checked
hook: in the Gita's list of offerings, some people offer their breath, and it sits in a row with everyone else's gift
carry: the breath again — every claim checked
tomorrow: the breath again — every claim checked

segments.voice: Yesterday, the breath again: a yoga manual said breath is tamed like a lion, slowly, and we kept its caution and checked its promise. Did a big health promise cross your path? Day one thousand three hundred twenty-six.

What would it mean to give a breath away? Not to hold it, or push it, or count it. To offer it, the way a person sets a flower down in front of an image or pours a spoon of ghee into a fire. In the fourth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna walks Arjuna through a long list of offerings that people make. Wealth, study, discipline, the restraint of the senses. And in the middle of the list, quietly, breath. Today: what the Gita does with the breath, and a claim about it that the list itself answers.
screen: `GIVE A BREATH AWAY?` → `A LIST OF OFFERINGS.` → `BREATH, IN THE MIDDLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, in paraphrase. Some, Krishna says, offer the in-breath into the out-breath, and the out-breath into the in-breath, holding the path of both, given over to the practice of breath. Read that slowly. The breath going in is poured into the breath going out, like an offering into a fire, and back again. Breathing itself becomes a yajna, a sacrifice. The ordinary thing the body does all day is treated as a gift. Then look at the company it keeps. Around that verse, the Gita lists others. Some offer their senses into the fire of restraint. Some offer their possessions. Some offer austerity, some offer study, some offer yoga. And then a short line that sums up the whole row: all of these know what sacrifice is. Now the claim. You'll sometimes hear that the Gita names breath control as the highest yoga, the secret above all others. Check it against the chapter. Breath is there, honored, given its own careful verse. But it stands in a row with study, with giving, with self-restraint. The list doesn't crown it. What the Gita adds is a direction. The point of the breath isn't what you get from it. It's what you give with it. Later, in the fifth chapter, the Gita mentions making the in-breath and out-breath even as they move within the nostrils, but there too, breath serves a larger aim: a person free of desire, fear and anger. So the claim shrinks, and the teaching grows. Breath isn't a secret weapon. In the Gita, it can be an offering.
screen: `IN-BREATH POURED INTO OUT-BREATH` · `BREATHING AS A SACRIFICE` · `ONE GIFT IN A ROW OF GIFTS` · `NOT WHAT YOU GET, BUT WHAT YOU GIVE`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let one breath be a gift. Sit comfortably and let the breath move on its own. Notice the breath in arriving, and let it flow into the breath out, without a seam. Then the breath out turning into the breath in. If it helps, picture the gentlest offering: something set down, not thrown. If you pray, you can offer your breathing, just as it is, to God, as some Hindus do. If you don't, you can simply let it go with thanks. The bell holds the time.
The breath again. In the Gita, some offer the in-breath into the out-breath, one gift in a row of many. Today's word.
Your line: the breath again — every claim checked. Today, before one ordinary task, take a breath and set it down as a gift. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-six.

howItsDone: Some Hindus treat daily actions, breathing among them, as offerings in the spirit of the Gita's fourth chapter, and the Gita's verses on breath are recited and studied in traditions of yoga.

fork.setup: you're Krishna, listing the ways people make offerings. where does breath go?
options: at the top, above everything else.
left out: it's only the body.
in the row, alongside study, giving and restraint.
fork.reveal: breath gets its own careful verse, in the middle of the list, and the Gita says all of these know what sacrifice is.

original.note: Sanskrit: sacrifice, offering. in Gita 4, breathing itself can be a yajna. some speakers say it closer to YUG-yuh.

trapdoor: what you thought: in the Gita, breath control is the secret above all others.
what it means: in chapter four, breath is one offering in a row of offerings, honored, not crowned.
what a scholar hears: prana poured into apana and back, breathing itself treated as yajna, a sacrifice.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 4.25–4.28 (offerings of the senses, possessions, austerity, yoga, study)
Bhagavad Gita 4.29 (some offer prana into apana and apana into prana, restraining both)
Bhagavad Gita 5.27–5.28 (making prana and apana even within the nostrils; free of desire, fear and anger)

notes: Gita 4.29: confirm the paraphrase 'offer the in-breath into the out-breath and the out-breath into the in-breath, restraining the course of both, devoted to breath control'. Commentators differ on which of prana/apana is the in-breath; the lesson follows the common reading (prana in, apana out) — a Keeper should confirm or soften.

Gita 4.33 (the offering of knowledge is called superior to material offerings) is deliberately not mentioned; the lesson says only that the list does not crown breath control. Check that this is a fair reading.
Original: pronunciation of yajna varies by region (YUG-nyuh, YUG-yuh, YAJ-nuh).
Practice line 'as some Hindus do' offering breathing to God: confirm this is fair and unforced.

Editor pass: the hook listed 'food' among the offerings; Gita 4.30 speaks of those who regulate their food, not an offering of food, so the hook list now matches the teach (wealth, study, discipline, restraint of the senses).
